editorials.title: The incoming ‘super’ El Niño will create chaos around the world – and we are far from ready for it
editorials.passage:
I f you think you have heard enough about the growing “super” El Niño, trust me, you are going to hear a lot more. What is happening in the equatorial Pacific is jaw-dropping and could well mark one of the biggest global weather upheavals in a millennium. It will spawn a string of weather catastrophes around our world in what remains of this year and in 2027, and there is no reason to think the UK will be immune.

To recap briefly, El Niño involves a heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural cycle termed the El Niño southern oscillation, which switches between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases. El Niños that see heating reach or exceed 2C are defined as “super” but this one, which is forecast to top-out at an astonishing 4C later this year, is so much bigger, the term “hyper” might be more appropriate.

El Niño is nothing new. Evidence for its existence extends back hundreds of millions of years and its ramifications have always been negative and disruptive. The difference today is that it is happening at a time when our world is heating more rapidly than ever before, and it is being supercharged as a result, leading to increasingly extreme weather.

Figuring out how much global heating alone is influencing El Niño is not straightforward, as its strength and other characteristics change naturally over time. Both El Niños and La Niñas, for example, have been steadily increasing in duration over the last 7,000 years. This is bad news in its own right, as it means the world’s weather is knocked out of kilter for even longer, but added to this, stronger El Niños are becoming more frequent as we continue to add CO 2 to the atmosphere.

There is no straightforward correlation between El Niño’s strength and the magnitude of impacts in any given part of the planet. But given the unprecedented amount of extra heat being added to the atmosphere over the Pacific, it would be reasonable to expect the world to experience exceptionally hazardous weather over the course of the next several months.

How, then, is the UK likely to fare? The Met Office has already warned of the increased likelihood of a stormy and wet autumn and early winter, so it would be judicious to start preparing now for flooding on a serious – perhaps even epic – scale. After all, the last big El Niño, in 2015–16, resulted in the most extreme UK floods on record . Stronger winds are also a big worry, as many trees weakened by this summer’s extreme drought conditions could be brought down in the powerful storms to come. A strong El Niño could also bring Arctic air to the UK later in the winter, although this is far from set in stone. Whether El Niño fosters more record-breaking heat next summer also remains to be seen.

But there are likely to be indirect impacts on the UK too, thanks to the devastating effects strong El Niños have on the global economy. While the great recession of 2008 resulted in global GDP reducing by around $2tn , the 1997–98 super-El Niño resulted in losses of $5.7tn. Much of this was due to the suppression of economic activity that can last for up to 14 years after a strong El Niño. The late-90s El Niño – the most powerful of the 20th century – peaked at 2.4C; the current one is already at 2.7C , meaning significant impacts on UK food security, cost of living and general economic wellbeing would not be a surprise.

However the UK fares in the coming months, its challenges are likely to be small beer compared with elsewhere on the planet . The effects of the strengthening El Niño are already being keenly felt, particularly across India, which is experiencing its weakest monsoon for 20 years. As El Niño peaks later this year, and slowly subsides, the west coast of South America and the western US can expect torrential rains, severe flooding and mudslides. Meanwhile, heatwaves, drought and wildfires will be the order of the day across the Amazon, south and south-east Asia and much of Australia. One tiny positive is that Atlantic hurricane activity tends to be damped down during El Niño years, but this is more than made up for by the revving up of Pacific typhoons.

California, in particular, is bracing itself for the worst, primarily because past super-El Niños have brought some of the wettest periods in the history of the state. This is because El Niño years tend to favour the formation of “atmospheric rivers” – streams of exceptional precipitation that track across the state from the Pacific for days at a time, dumping colossal amounts of rain. Such conditions contributed to the great flood of 1862, which left a vast area of the state under water, including a 480km-long stretch of the Central Valley. The biggest worry is that this unprecedented El Niño will see the realisation of a megastorm worst-case scenario known as the ARkStorm . If it does, expect millions of homes and businesses to be flooded, long-term damage to infrastructure, and economic losses totalling almost $1tn. Given, too, that tech companies would be severely impacted, the knock-on effects could result in another hammer blow to the global economy.

The effects of the El Niño will be felt well into 2027, almost certainly ensuring that next year is the hottest ever recorded, possibly by some margin. It would not be unexpected for the average global temperature to reach at least 1.6C above preindustrial levels, and quite possibly 1.7C or more.

Every tonne of CO 2 added to the atmosphere helps El Niños get stronger, and it would be nice to imagine that the coming monster might prove a wake-up call. But no. Governments continue to row back on green policies and fossil fuel corporations still plan for expansion.

As this year’s super-El Niño looms large, the UK government advises us to stock up on food while it prepares to greenlight the extraction of more fossil fuels from the North Sea. Cognitive dissonance doesn’t even begin to describe the idiocy of such thinking. You couldn’t make it up.

Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World: A History and Future of the Climate Crisis (HarperCollins Publishers, £20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com . Delivery charges may apply.

editorials.title: AI safety requires more than just slowing our pace
editorials.passage:
I t has been a week of high drama in AI, precipitated by the resignation of the AI safety researcher Jacob Coxon from Anthropic . This followed several weeks of increasingly lurid and disturbing revelations about the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident.

My inbox yesterday included a message from Business Insider with the subject line: “AI doomsday debate reaches boiling point”.

Now, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has written a 3,800-word, reassuringly phrased letter titled “We Must Pace the Frontier,” describing his proposals for avoiding (or at least postponing) doomsday. Sam Altman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, Demis Hassabis of Google Deepmind, and Satya Nadella of Microsoft have all expressed support.

You may be forgiven for not immediately understanding what “pace the frontier” means. (My first image was of Amodei walking deep in thought along the Finnish–Russian border.)

The phrase also appeared in July’s “Pacing the Frontier” open letter, signed by 1,386 employees of frontier AI labs, including Amodei himself.

While that letter may have upset the industry’s PR executives with its signatories noting “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling superintelligent AI systems” and asserting that “building things smarter than humans … is, objectively, an insane and suicidal thing to do”, Amodei’s monograph goes out of its way to mollify investors.

The notion of pacing the frontier seems to come from Formula 1: when conditions become too dangerous for racing, a pace car comes onto the track and all the other cars have to follow it as a safe speed. Progress continues, without the danger.

Amodei writes: “To be clear, pacing does not mean halting model training or technical progress.”

Amodei’s letter is prompted by his concern that “AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by ... recursive self-improvement.” It’s as if he and Sam find themselves driving their F1 cars at 200mph neck-and-neck heading into the first corner, only to realize it’s covered in ice and they have no steering wheel. No wonder they want to slow down.

In brief, Amodei’s proposal has three parts. The first is to have third-party AI system evaluators working inside each company, with full access to the systems; he commits Anthropic to this plan now, without waiting for the government to require it.

The second part of the plan asks all the frontier AI companies in “democratic countries” to “establish common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress”, with government regulation where needed. The third part would include “authoritarian countries” in a broader compact.

Here, Amodei goes out of his way to reassure those in Washington who see America’s lead in AI as its most important geopolitical asset.

On a casual reading, there are many reasons to believe that Amodei is calling for a general slowdown in the rate of progress. He talks about “limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress” and “some kind of ‘speed limit’ on the rate of recursive self- improvement (RSI)”. He says: “Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain.”

Slowing down would give companies a bit more time to work on safety; Amodei talks about one to two years of extra time for research on interpretability, alignment, and better testing methods.

Let me pause here to respond to Amodei’s critics who say it’s just a bid to cement Anthropic’s lead with the help of government intervention. This is nonsense. In fact, the Wikipedia page on pacing in F1 races says it “eliminates any time and distance advantage that a leading driver may have had over the remaining field of competitors”.

Having said that, I think the pacing metaphor is completely misguided.

We cannot set a slower rate of progress for capabilities and then hope that provides enough time to get the safety right. The safety requirements are non-negotiable. We must set the safety requirements first, and further progress occurs only when they are met.

Imagine if Boeing said: “We’re going to introduce a new plane every year, and we hope that provides enough time for some flight tests to be completed and for the results to be good.”

We would say: “No, you have that backwards; you can introduce a new plane only when it has passed all the tests and the government has issued an airworthiness certification. If that takes more than a year, so be it.”

A more careful reading of the document suggests that Amodei agrees with this objection. For example, he says that rules should be of the form: “If models have capability X, then they need to be accompanied by certifications of alignment properties Y and Z.”

In other words, we set safety requirements, and developers have to show that they meet those requirements. This is in fact the “red lines” approach that AI safety researchers have been calling for.

And it means that if developers can’t figure out how to meet the safety requirements, then they will have to halt. It would be, in F1 terminology, a red flag and not a pacing car.

There is no plausible alternative. Recursive self-improvement leading to superintelligent AI raises the risk of the irreversible loss of human control. The acceptable risk level for loss of control is perhaps one in 100m per year, not the one in 10 or one in five that the AI CEOs currently estimate.

And remember “the complete absence of credible plans for controlling superintelligent AI systems”. At some point, progress along this technology path will halt, not because further progress is impossible, but because further progress is untenable when the technology is intrinsically unsafe. Humanity has a right to protect itself.

There is huge resistance to this conclusion. We have already sunk trillions of dollars into the current technology path and plan to sink trillions more. But the sunk cost fallacy is just that: if we double down on a mistake, it’s still a mistake.

The present level of attention to AI risk, the unanimity of the leading technology executives, and the forthcoming Trump–Xi summit give us a real opportunity to choose a different path. We must take it.

Stuart Russell is a distinguished professor of computer science at University of California, Berkeley, the president of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence and a Guardian US columnist

editorials.title: Thank goodness Labour’s ‘shambolic’ plan to reorganise local councils has been paused. What was it thinking?
editorials.passage:
S hock reverberated through England’s councils last week. “Beggars belief!” “Shambolic!” council leaders protested to the Local Government Information Unit (LGIU), which says: “We’ve never before heard such expletives. They’re apoplectic, incandescent.” And they have every right to be.

The government has slammed the brakes on its unexpected reorganisation of local councils. This almost certainly ends the one-size-fits-all, politically damaging remapping of England’s councils , which was never forewarned in Labour’s manifesto.

Councils hired extra staff to manage gigantic mergers and changes on the running of social care, waste collection, libraries, special educational needs, children in care, roads and parks – absolutely everything sliced and diced, with hundreds of thousands moving jobs under new brass plates.

Take Worcestershire county council. It just hired a local government reorganisation director on about £120,000 a year who started in August to abolish six district councils , dividing the county into two new unitary authorities. But like everywhere else that’s paused , subject to “ rapid review ”, much of it is dead in the water.

Why this emergency stop? Facing legal challenges from objectors over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk, the local government secretary, Angela Rayner, received new legal advice that the reorganisation may not comply with law. From the start, I could see no political purpose in her launching this fiendishly complicated restructuring that has now crashed. On the contrary, it would have done Labour and the Liberal Democrats considerable harm. Under the original plan, progressive-voting urban strongholds would vanish as separate entities, absorbed into surrounding county councils with historically more conservative electorates.

Rayner is not to blame for this. Neither is Steve Reed, who took over the brief before Burnham reinstated her to it. “Angela did not come into government to reorganise local councils,” her people say indignantly. Her focus and purpose are fixed on housing, as the motor to drive growth. This was forced on her. By whom and why?

It’s yet another misconceived Treasury pet project foisted on a new government. Those closest to events have told me that the Treasury threatened to refuse funds for councils or capital for her housing targets unless she agreed to its plan. It took down a dusty 2020 PriceWaterhouseCoopers report from its shelves that purported to show that abolishing district councils and creating huge unitary authorities of up to 500,000 citizens throughout England would save money. Not very local.

Whose idea was it originally? The then Conservative-dominated County Councils Network, which commissioned the PwC report, promising cost savings if district councils were absorbed into county councils. How much? The small print of that six-year-old report suggests a mere £2.9bn – over five years. Then factor in the costs in wasted staff time: disruption, endless meetings, recruitment, unpicking contracts and energy not spent on myriad acute problems.

Treasury orthodoxy always thinks bigger is better and cheaper. Hampshire, with its district councils, is no better or worse run than, say, Shropshire or Buckinghamshire unitaries, Prof Tony Travers of the London School of Economics tells me. The House of Commons library finds no evidence that unitary councils save money compared with the current two-tier system.

If there is no profit, then look at the loss. Dwindling interest in community activism has led to a decrease in volunteers, members of political parties, trade unions, churches and sports clubs, those who keep society alive. So let’s not lose platoons of district councillors who help hold the social fabric together: these are people who know their communities, and whom residents know they can turn to. Experts at the Localis thinktank believe that abolishing district councils means “unsustainable workloads on remaining councillors”. There has been a huge reduction in the number of councillors in England over the past 60 years. Last year, Localis warned that nine in 10 councillors in shire areas could be culled by the reorganisation. A 2024 poll showed that in England people were twice as likely to trust local politicians to improve their areas as they were national politicians. There is clear evidence that councillors shore up people’s confidence in democracy.

Andy Burnham’s devolution of powers to mayors (or strategic authorities) across every region will move much faster if these council reorganisation plans are permanently shelved. Yes, it means that some places will have three layers of government – district, county and mayoral. But surely that is preferable to sweeping away local representation. There are worse things than having more local people getting involved as councillors, helping to run and shape their communities.

Even some who think the unitary principle is “a better system”, as Vince Maple, the Labour leader of Medway council, says, also think redrawing borders is “no panacea” for councils devastated, like his, by a “91% cut in the revenue support grant after 2010”. Under these plans, Maple tells me, they were preparing mergers for all the complex ways that next-door councils do things – from professional approaches to social care to contentious rates for councillors’ remuneration and allowances. Unitaries may be better in principle, but he concedes reorganisation may not be worth the upheaval.

Who should pay for this fiasco of a plan, and the chaos of its abrupt pause? The Treasury, who imposed it without due legal scrutiny. I trust the National Audit Office will record this classic case of Whitehall’s urge to create new organograms instead of solving practical problems on the ground. The former Tory MP Eric Pickles, who as local government secretary wielded an axe over council funding, had only one good thought : “I intend to keep a loaded pearl-handled revolver in my drawer, and the first civil servant who suggests local government reorganisation will be shot.”

Apply that thought to every department – the NHS is a frequent victim. Learn from the expletives emitted by the usually quiet battalions of public servants who keep services running, even amid this needless pandemonium.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

editorials.title: Sweden’s far right is down, but not yet out. Left and centre leaders must seize this opportunity
editorials.passage:
A fter the previous Swedish general election, in 2022, the leaders of the two biggest Swedish parties made a risky decision. Jimmie Åkesson , the leader of the far-right Sweden Democrats (SD), chose to support the rightwing minority government of the Moderate party prime minister Ulf Kristersson , while Magdalena Andersson, the Social Democrats’ leader, decided to copy the “Danish model” in an attempt to regain power. In both cases, the strategy led to electoral loss but political success .

After the general election in the country on Sunday, the Social Democrats (often referred to as S or Sap), in common with its Danish counterparts, will probably lead the new government despite an electoral defeat, losing roughly 2%, its worst result since 1908. The party’s return to power is purely a result of Swedish bloc politics and the victories of its likely coalition partners : the Left party (V), the Green party and the Center party (C), which all increased their support by 1.5%, 1.7% and 0.4% respectively. Together, this left bloc has a majority of just three seats in the new parliament. So while Andersson will probably return to power, she is also in a very vulnerable position.

While the three leftwing parties agree on a lot of socioeconomic issues, particularly undoing some of the worst rightwing policies of the past years and investing more in the public sector, they hold very different views on issues like crime and immigration. Should Andersson continue to demand strict immigration rules and link crime to immigration, this could lead to significant tensions in her coalition, similar to those that her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen, faced in her first government.

At the same time the small Center party, the least leftwing of the left bloc, has ruled out a (formal) coalition with the “radical” Left party, and will want to protect the market from too much state intervention. This will create further tensions within the left bloc in a probable minority government. Given that format and the inevitable internal tensions, a majority of just three seats would require almost unrealistic levels of discipline for the minority government to sit out a full term.

On the other side of the political spectrum, the Sweden Democrats had their first loss in a national parliamentary election. Still, there is little reason to assume that Åkesson will face a backlash. First, he was the only leader who had any significance to a majority of his party’s electorate. Second, his support strategy worked: the Sweden Democrats is now completely normalised within the right bloc, as the leader of the Moderate party (or M), Kristersson, had already announced before the election that the Sweden Democrats would be part of a next rightwing government. Third, the party’s nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.

We should also not forget that the 2022 election campaign offered the perfect political context for the Sweden Democrats, given that it was dominated by two themes: immigration and the acceptance of the Sweden Democrats. As we know from other elections (such as in the Netherlands in 2023), when opposition to immigration and the acceptance of the far right dominate the political agenda, the far right wins big. This time round, those topics were still there, but they did not dominate the campaign – in fact, no single issue did. On top of that, the Sweden Democrats were linked to some scandals close to the election, which might have further decreased support for the party. Still, it held on to 78% of its 2022 electorate, more than the centre-right Moderates (59%) and centre-left Social Democrats (73%).

While Andersson may try to convince her party, and herself, that the “Danish model” has worked, she should take a better look at her small neighbour to the west. The Danish Social Democratic party has hit historical lows in national and local elections (notably in the capital, Copenhagen). And although Frederiksen in Denmark is such a convincing nativist that even far-right leaders in other countries hail her as an example, the far right is barely less popular than before – just more divided.

Interestingly, while Andersson thanked the youth and student branches for their great work in her election night speech, the Social Democrats scored significantly lower among first-time voters than among the electorate as a whole (21% and 28%, respectively). In contrast, the Left and the Greens did significantly better among the youth. This reflects a development we see across Europe , namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties. The Social Democrats were the most popular among Swedes with non-European roots, however, gaining no less than 38% of support within this growing part of the electorate. No doubt this group is also not looking for more nativist policies and rhetoric.

In short, even if the Social Democrats have regained power because of the “Danish model”, which is in itself debatable, this same strategy will be a risk for the new coalition and for the electoral future of the party. Rather than continuing to be a “moderate” or “sensible” alternative to the Moderates, Andersson should fully commit to a progressive political agenda, both on socioeconomic and socio-cultural policies. That way she not only has a better chance of holding her coalition together, but also might make her party attractive to new and younger voters again.

Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author of The Far Right Today

editorials.title: Europe’s summer emergency was a dire warning for Australia. What can be learned before it’s too late?
editorials.passage:
B ack in April 2004, in the shadow of the previous European summer, I started work at Downing Street advising the British prime minister on climate change. The 2003 heatwave had killed an estimated 70,000 people across Europe. Many were older people, in homes and neighbourhoods ill-equipped for prolonged heat.

In May this year, I walked through Bordeaux with my 83-year-old mother-in-law in 38C heat. I saw how quickly heat changes the terms of ordinary life. Streets emptied. Shade became essential. The question was not simply the temperature, but whether people could work, sleep or remain safely at home.

That was the European spring. By summer, 42,000 hectares around Gironde and Arcachon surrounding the city had burned. France experienced its worst fires since 1949.

In June, during the Tour de Suisse, the Italian champion cyclist Elisa Longo Borghini suffered heatstroke. She struggled afterwards to remember the final climb. If extreme heat can overwhelm an elite athlete, we should understand the danger it presents to us all.

Europe’s warning is relevant to every Australian city.

Extreme heat is not merely uncomfortable weather. Between 2000 and 2018, extreme heat caused more deaths in Australia than all our bushfires, floods, storms and cyclones combined. Yet it remains under-recognised because it leaves little visible destruction and its effects are often recorded as heart, kidney or respiratory illness rather than heat itself.

And risk is not evenly shared. Older people, particularly those living alone, people with chronic illness, outdoor workers and people in poorly cooled homes are more exposed. As we age, our ability to sense heat, sweat effectively and regulate body temperature can diminish, while thirst can become a less reliable prompt. Staying hydrated must be a habit throughout a hot day, not an afterthought when work is finished.

This has cultural as well as policy implications. We should challenge the idea that a cold beer is enough to manage the impact of hard physical labour in dangerous heat. Or its quieter twin: the carer skipping her own break to help someone else. Nagging your older relatives and checking on neighbours could save a life.

Australians understand seasonal preparation. We do it for bushfires. Governments plan, agencies coordinate, volunteers are mobilised and communities are encouraged to act before danger arrives.

We should bring the same mindset to extreme heat.

The risk is not confined to bushland at the edge of our cities. It may be a hot top-floor apartment, a home with no shade or breeze, or a worksite. It affects the postcodes of Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth differently, but is now a national test of whether our homes, cities and services are ready for the climate we have.

Here in New South Wales, the state government and its agencies have recognised heat as a growing risk and strengthened arrangements for declared heatwaves, including clearer roles and updated warnings.

The government can build on these foundations. Our Heat Stress Spotlight Report identifies a critical gap. NSW has improved its response once a heatwave is declared, but dangerous heat does not always meet a formal threshold. Isolated very hot days and heat combined with high humidity can be dangerous too. Emergency arrangements must be complemented by a coordinated, annual system of preparation.

We believe NSW Health can lead a seasonal heat plan through the hotter months. It could help agencies prepare, ensure warnings are clear and trusted, and direct support to those at greatest risk. Exposure to extreme heat can also be reduced through cooler housing, better shade and tree cover, stronger thermal protections for renters and social and Aboriginal housing tenants, and effective workplace heat plans.

NSW also needs consistent public data on heat-related illness and deaths. If we cannot see the burden clearly, we cannot judge whether our responses reach those who need it to prevent avoidable harm.

Responding to hotter summers is work government cannot do alone. Resilient Sydney has helped place heat resilience on the public agenda, including through the Greater Sydney Heat Smart City Plan . Sweltering Cities has made the everyday reality of heat in homes, streets and suburbs impossible to ignore, especially for people least able to avoid it. Their work deserves recognition. It also shows why state government, councils, health services, employers and community organisations need to work together.

Bushfires have flames. Floods leave visible damage. Extreme heat acts silently, accumulating in homes, streets and bodies over days and nights. By the time it becomes visible in emergency departments or mortality figures, the opportunity to prevent much of the harm has passed.

We treat bushfire as a seasonal certainty. It is time we treated heat the same way: by preparing early, coordinating well and protecting people before the next heatwave reaches a street near you.

Nick Rowley is chair of the NSW Net Zero Commission

editorials.title: Burnham must establish an inquiry into Britain’s role in the Gaza genocide
editorials.passage:
History does not really repeat itself, but, as the saying frequently attributed to Mark Twain goes, it often rhymes. Take, for example, Britain’s involvement in the Middle East since the turn of the century. It took six years before the British government established an independent committee of Privy Counsellors to examine the United Kingdom’s involvement in the 2003 Iraq war, and an additional seven years before Sir John Chilcot and other members of the inquiry committee published their damning findings that former Prime Minister Tony Blair had misled the public and his own government.

The Inquiry found that the UK chose to join the invasion before peaceful options had been exhausted, that Saddam Hussein did not, in fact, pose an imminent threat and that Blair had deliberately exaggerated the danger and then promised former United States President George Bush: “I will be with you, whatever.” It also found that Britain’s intelligence agencies had produced “flawed information”, that Blair had ignored warnings about what would happen in Iraq after the invasion, and that the government had not tried hard enough to keep a tally of Iraqi civilian casualties, which, according to Iraq Body Count, amounts to between 187,499 and 211,046 deaths.

Prime Minister Gordon Brown would not have established the inquiry committee without unrelenting pressure from within Parliament and civil society, and it was only due to these persistent demands that the truth finally saw the light of day (even though Tony Blair has still not been held to account).

Fast forward to the Gaza genocide. In June 2025, former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn proposed a bill for a full, independent, public inquiry into Britain’s role in the genocide in Gaza. This inquiry committee would consider any UK military, economic or political cooperation with Israel since October 2023, including the sale, supply or use of weapons, surveillance aircraft and Royal Air Force bases, while also having the power to question ministers and officials about decisions taken in relation to UK involvement.

The bill secured the support of more than 50 MPs. However, when it reached a second reading, Keir Starmer’s government blocked its passage. The government said “there is no need for an inquiry” and that “such an inquiry would be unnecessary as there is no confusion about UK military operations in Gaza.”

In response, Jeremy Corbyn decided to hold a public tribunal in the tradition of the Russell Tribunal organised by the great British philosopher Bertrand Russell in 1966 to investigate US war crimes in Vietnam. Corbyn invited Shahd Hammouri, an international law lecturer at the University of Kent, and me to join the Tribunal panel, and the hearings were held on September 4-5, 2025, in Church House, Westminster.

We heard 29 testimonies from witnesses, journalists and survivors of the Gaza genocide, as well as a range of international law experts, lawyers, medical doctors and whistleblowers. At the time, the official death toll in Gaza was nearing 65,000, of whom almost 20,000 were children. With more than 150,000 injured, Gaza had become the home of the largest cohort of child amputees in the world. Almost 80 percent of the buildings in Gaza had either been damaged or destroyed, including more than 90 percent of housing, 97 percent of schools, 33 of 36 hospitals, and every single university in the Strip.

The two days of hearings were among the most difficult in my life, given the emotional toll of listening to so many horrific testimonies. In addition to testimony after testimony describing the extent of the British government’s complicity in the mass murder and destruction, we also heard from a whistleblower about the culture of deception – to cover up the government’s wrongdoings – that had taken over the corridors of power. In the subsequent months, we analysed the findings and concluded that Britain had played a vital role in Israeli military operations in Gaza, including but not limited to:

The sale, supply and transfer of weapons that have been used to extinguish human life and destroy vital infrastructure in Gaza, the West Bank and beyond. This included individual export licences issued directly to Israel, as well as the indirect supply of components for F-35 fighter jets. The use of Royal Air Force surveillance flights over Gaza and British airbases to facilitate the transport, refuelling and maintenance of military equipment. The provision of political and diplomatic support, which has empowered Israel, enabling it to commit atrocities with impunity. This support has included the dehumanisation of Palestinians in political rhetoric, the justification of Israel’s actions, the hosting of Israeli officials, the failure to uphold the authority and decisions of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC), and the demonisation of international solidarity, including the proscription of Palestine Action as a terrorist group.

In March 2026, Corbyn submitted the Tribunal’s findings to the ICC, encouraging the court to interview government ministers regarding British complicity in war crimes. Since then, he has continued to demand a full, official, independent public inquiry into any cooperation between the UK and Israel since October 2023.

Corbyn knows that the Tribunal he organised is no substitute for a full, public, independent inquiry, and given that there is a new prime minister in Number 10 who said Labour “got it wrong” over Gaza, Corbyn wanted to know whether the current Labour government would finally commit to investigating Britain’s role in the genocide. Expressions of regret are certainly important, but if justice is the goal, then the UK public requires both truth and accountability.

Last week, the bill that Keir Starmer’s government blocked back in June 2025 was once again brought before Parliament, and once again the government blocked MPs from voting on it. The Burnham government’s decision to postpone the vote on Corbyn’s Bill is reminiscent of the way previous governments postponed the establishment of an inquiry to investigate the Iraq war. It appears that, like previous UK governments, the current government’s strategy is to demur and delay, with the goal of sending the Gaza inquiry bill to purgatory.

The problem for Burnham is that, today, he and other members of the ruling elite no longer have the power to define the “common sense” through which Gaza is understood. Public opinion on Israel has shifted, as the huge pro-Palestinian marches and opinion polls demonstrate. The majority of the UK population knows that Israel is committing a genocide and that it has been able to do so, in part, because of the support of Western governments. While the US and Germany were undoubtedly the most enthusiastic supporters – providing Israel with the lethal mechanisms and the diplomatic shield to carry out mass killings – the public also understands that Britain has played a vital role.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband’s recent – and I would say courageous – announcement that the UK government would ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements and sanction companies and individuals supporting settlement activity is a very important first step. Yet, it does not absolve the UK government of its alleged complicity in atrocity crimes.

The disturbing testimonies we heard during the Tribunal underscore the importance of formal scrutiny. The vote on Corbyn’s bill was postponed last week, but the need to reveal the role the British government played in Israel’s genocidal onslaught is not going away. Burnham and Miliband have a historic opportunity to prove that this new government is committed to the principles of international law and currently face a straightforward choice: Continue to block efforts to expose the truth and seek accountability, or break with the past and stand on the right side of history. History often rhymes, but it does not have to.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Can a party be leftist and Zionist?
editorials.passage:
Ahead of Israel’s October 27 elections, Israel’s Young Democrats, the youth wing of the newly formed Democrats party, are seeking foreign allies. They recently announced a joint campaign with the Young Greens of Austria to support “progressive voices on the ground and work with them towards a sustainable peace”.

Meanwhile, another youth group described as “leftist”, Hamahanot Haolim (the Ascending Camps), is exploring plans to build a new kibbutz in the occupied West Bank, near Jericho.

When questioned about the impact on the Palestinian population, the group’s director, Ilan Gazit, explained that since Israeli settlements are being built regardless, “the left” should make sure it is Israeli “leftists”, not far-right settlers, who populate them. “We aren’t ashamed of this, and we aren’t hiding it,” he said.

These two youth movements and their foreign sympathisers appear to treat “leftist Zionism” as a coherent political identity. But can a party, a movement, or an individual be both leftist and Zionist?

The short answer, from a Palestinian and anti‑colonial perspective, is no. So why is it touted in Israel and beyond as a legitimate ideological belief? Because it is a political technology designed to shield Zionism from any critique while preserving the structures of oppression.

The question about the viability of “leftist Zionism” is not new. Zionism emerged as an organised Jewish nationalist movement in Europe in the 19th century. At its core was the aim of establishing a Jewish national home, an idea shaped by European nationalism, European anti-Semitism, and colonial expansion.

Its early political architects advanced two connected projects: redefining Judaism as a national identity and colonising Palestine. Theodor Herzl, a Hungarian Jewish journalist who is seen as the founder of Zionism, was motivated not by religious zeal, as he espoused secularism, but by the growing anti-Semitism in Europe.

After Herzl’s death in 1904, leftist ideas entered the movement as various socialist factions rose to dominance within the World Zionist Organization and in early settler communities in Palestine itself.

But these leftist elements were not driven by a genuine commitment to class-based struggle and internationalism. Rather, they used a socialist vocabulary to justify a settler-colonial nation-building project, carried out through kibbutzim, labour unions, and diplomacy.

Whatever position early Zionists staked out on the political spectrum, what the movement ultimately produced — the state of Israel — was in direct contradiction with the anti-colonial, anti-racist politics the left was supposed to stand for.

In 1975, the United Nations General Assembly acknowledged this by adopting Resolution 3379, declaring that “Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination”. The resolution was revoked in 1991, after sustained pressure from Israel and its allies and in the wake of the Soviet collapse.

The debate about “leftist Zionism” continues till today. The issue is not whether individual Zionists can hold progressive views on particular social or economic questions. Some might.

The real question is whether a political project organised around building and sustaining a state premised on Jewish supremacy through ethnic cleansing, dispossession, apartheid, and now genocide can be reconciled with the left’s foundational commitments: equity, anti‑racism, decolonisation, and social justice for everyone.

When considering the historical record, it is important to note that for decades, Israel was governed by parties that would self-describe as “leftist”.

Mapai was established as a Labour Zionist party in 1930, led by David Ben-Gurion. It became the dominant force within early Zionist politics and the principal architect of the pre‑state and early institutions, including the Haganah, which carried out various terrorist attacks and massacres against the Palestinians.

Mapai governed Israel well into the 1960s, giving way to the Labour Party, which dominated Israeli politics until the 1990s.

Labour Zionism spoke the language of workers’ solidarity while building institutions that excluded Palestinians by design.

The Histadrut, Israel’s dominant trade‑union confederation, was founded in 1920 as an instrument of the Zionist “conquest of labour”: a project designed to build Jewish settlements by systematically displacing Palestinian workers from the economy and reducing dependence on Indigenous labour. After 1948, this exclusion was institutionalised: Palestinian workers were either barred from membership outright or confined to second‑class status for decades, denied voting rights and meaningful representation even as they paid union fees.

Today, even when on paper Palestinians should have the same rights as Jewish Israeli workers, in practice, they do not. Collective bargaining agreements in key sectors, such as construction , are consistently not applied to them because their employment is rendered unstable, informal, and “temporary” by design. In this way, the Histadrut functions less as a defender of workers’ rights and more as a key actor in reproducing a settler‑colonial order that segregates, exploits, and disempowers Palestinian labour.

The school system set up by early Labour governments functioned as an instrument of ideological formation: forging Jewish national consciousness while erasing Palestinian presence, and recasting settlement as national redemption rather than colonisation.

The kibbutz and moshav movements, the flagship institutions of Labour Zionism, were central to the project of land theft and displacement. Many kibbutzim, due to their location, served as staging grounds for Haganah operations in 1948, including the depopulation of nearby Palestinian villages, making the settlement map itself part of the operational infrastructure of the Nakba.

Despite the long historical record of crimes committed by Mapai and Labour governments against the Palestinians, many leftists in the West continue to fall for the “leftist” label within the context of Israeli politics. They appear to believe that what is happening in Palestine could be solely blamed on Israel’s right-wing political forces led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Campaigns like that of the Young Greens of Austria and Israel’s Young Democrats seemingly reinforce this misguided belief. In the end, their ultimate aim is not to amplify “progressive voices” or deliver a “just peace” to the Palestinians, but to impose a political category – “leftist Zionist” – that is, in essence, incoherent and contradictory.

The constant reference to a “far‑right Netanyahu government” does real political work. It implies that a “Zionist left” could be a credible progressive alternative, one that is capable of changing the colonial reality Palestinians live under and one that is not to blame for Israeli crimes.

That framing lets the underlying structure – Israel’s settler colonialism – off the hook, treating it as a policy choice of the Israeli far right specifically rather than the logic of Zionism itself.

Palestinians do not need political theory to see the truth. Generations of them know, in their flesh, that there is no difference between Zionism on the left and Zionism on the right when it comes to their dispossession. The occupation did not start with Netanyahu, and a change in government will not end it.

Any leftist party in Europe or beyond that wants to remain aligned with its own values has one path. It should listen to Palestinians, follow and support forces like the Green Party of England and Wales in naming Zionism for what it is: a racist, settler-colonial ideology. Not a policy to be reformed, but an ideology to be abolished.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

editorials.title: Novelist and professor Saikat Majumdar on humanities education in a post-truth world
editorials.passage:
The bitterest battles in the world today are being fought in the humanities and the imaginative social sciences. This isn’t entirely new. Emotions, ideas, beliefs, faith, and ideology have always been the most violent and sensitive points of contact – no less than land, wealth, food, technology, the material body, and other issues that might belong to the natural and the harder social sciences. Human health, freedom, and development have always required both, without any hierarchy between them. That is one of the key reasons we study both the humanities and the natural sciences – and the social formations that turn individuals into communities.

Most university subjects, in their modern forms, can be traced back to the European Enlightenment. New ways of thinking, from Newtonian physics and Cartesian philosophy created a faith in science and reason. A rational appraisal of reality shaped many things that we take for granted today – from positivism in the social sciences to realism and interiority in literature. Older knowledge forms, ranging from philosophy to medicine to literature, got new centres of gravity during this period of radical modernity. It also brought a large-scale reorganisation of the institutions of knowledge and learning, particularly in their new secular formations. The modern Western research university was established through the intervention of Wilhelm von Humboldt in Germany, and graduate schools came into being, through the intervention of figures like Charles Eliot Norton at Harvard and Daniel Coit Gilman at Johns Hopkins.

Enlightenment in the colonies turned out to be a violent and contentious affair. “The night of the sword and the bullet was followed by the morning of the chalk and the blackboard,” wrote Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o. Gayatri Chakravarty Spivak compared postcolonial culture to children of rape, reminding us that one can hate the act but not the progeny born of it. In the end, the modernities of Europe were richly modified to create indigenous modernities that were resistant, celebratory, and revisionist. Just two notable examples from India: the Bengal Renaissance in the 19th century with its social reforms, scientific culture, and literary movements; and later, the revolutionary Progressive Writers’ Movement in early 20th century Urdu and Hindi literature, which offered a unique, subcontinental expansion of anticolonial literary modernism. Our public universities, too, have derived from this modernity – or rather from the distorted version of it that was practised by the colonial administration and ideology, what many have identified as a clerk-training, examination-driven model.

But the Truth of the Enlightenment, held up by its philosophy, science and technology, also turned out to be claustrophobic. Its colour was too White, its sex too Male, its orientation too Straight, its status too Bourgeois. When it came to Indian modernities, the White was replaced by the Savarna but everything else remained pretty much the same. It would not be too long before the technological advances of capitalist culture would lead to class exploitation and the devastation of the environment.

Throughout the 20th century, the sensitive and the rebellious questioned, critiqued, and wrestled with the Truth. Western reason’s claim of Truth was taken apart by feminists, anti-class and anti-caste thinkers, and theorists of race and colonialism. Truth was examined and challenged – but never abandoned altogether.

Suddenly, what we have now in the 21st century is both the spectre and the reality of the Post-Truth world. Truth doesn’t matter anymore. Only opinions, emotions, and feelings do, often fanned by the wilderness of mob justice. For a vast majority of people, reason and expertise have become dirty words. And one can see why. Globalisation and liberalisation worldwide, and the liberal and neoliberal cultures that enabled and benefited from them, excluded vast numbers of people, left them in their rural, working-class peripheries, in poverty and ignorance. Liberalism had cosied up too close to capitalism and had failed to be inclusive in spite of its grand vision. Those left out turned to unreason, prejudice, and bigotry. Charismatic dictators blazed their ways. 2016 led the way, with the election of Donald Trump and the British exit from the European Union. Both events were a backlash against the liberal world order, and its faith in reason, knowledge, and expertise.

This is our world now. While we remain preoccupied with rising waves of data, digitisation, and artificial intelligence – forces from the world of science and technology – popular action and even democratic choices are being increasingly driven by emotions, symbolism, and crucially, identity. Identity rooted in religion, race, caste – and in more complex ways, gender and sexuality. Everything that is in the domain of the humanities and the softer social sciences. The study of language and rhetoric, religious studies, the qualitative understanding of race, class, caste, and gender.

The greatest of today’s battles are ideological. “Ideology”, Mao had said, “is the greatest weapon.” The 20th century learned this lesson almost as immediately as they faced the deadlock of a mutually destructive military war. With nuclear power freezing martial stalemate, the battle turned to mind, ideology, and most potently, culture. Both the CIA and the KGB turned to the sponsorship of literary magazines and language institutes. The 21st-century superpower, China, has heavily invested in liberal arts colleges nationwide and Confucius Institutes worldwide to spread the soft power of Chinese language, culture, philosophy, and history. Thanks to paranoid cyber-vigilance, Western ideas now have very limited rights of entry into the country even as they aim for the American structure of liberal arts education. Educational policy in India today has been no different, with the greatest stamp of ideology being enacted through the humanities – history, philosophy, languages.

This is the terribly dubious importance of the humanities that disturbs me deeply as a humanist. To see the lingering shadow of the moment where the symbolism of a temple wins votes over the economics of real jobs – and to sigh in relief as that pitfall is narrowly avoided. The questions and debates that should belong to the genuine historian have been taken over in the streets, YouTube rants and WhatsApp gyaan. Language and symbolism – what is “freedom”, and who is an “outsider” – profoundly literary and philosophical ideas – shape political rhetoric more so than the language of economics or science: budgets, healthcare and welfare. Even the methods of the humanities, such as that of social relativism, are taken over by reactionary forces. The French philosopher Bruno Latour illustrated this while pointing out Right Wing activists who called global warming a “social construct” – much the way liberal humanists have described gender and sexuality.

The humanities, I repeat, are more urgent than ever before. But it is an urgency and an importance that depresses me as a humanist. As a humanist, I wish more people would respond to the caveats of science – the doom of global warming, the statistics and economics of job creation. I long for people to turn away from the falsity of language and aesthetic symbolism, fake claims of history, dangerous philosophies of the self and groups.

This is where you, the students come in to make the difference. We have seen intriguing duplicities in the architecture of liberal arts education both on the part of government and industry. The quest for the kind of interdisciplinary liberal education that can solve corporate problems but which is not liberal in the ethical or the political sense of the term. Critical enough to create wealth but critical enough to question power. I trust that you will enter the world of the humanities in this space of liberal arts education – and leave it to enter the larger world – without these chains. And if you do, as humanists, you will assume tremendous power and even greater responsibility.

It’s all about taking hold of the narrative and changing it as your true conscience tells you. Narrative, as a device, belongs to literature and history. But just the way the term “creative” was taken over by the marketing and accounts people – “creative” campaigns, and dangerously, “creative book keeping” – the reality and practice of narrative are mired today in the narrow battle of identity and ideology. But as humanists, no one will know better than you the complexities and paradoxes of identity and ideology. You’ll do this for your final papers and your theses; the big challenge will be to work with them in life, the workplace, your community, even your school and housing community WhatsApp groups.

As long as there is humanity, the humanities will be central – for better or for worse. Artificial Intelligence, at least in the arc of the future we can see, will merely reflect the virtues and vices of humankind. The writers of AI algorithms are but humans, and they carry the biases and liberalisms of humans. A recent study has revealed the deep prejudices behind the images generated by a popular AI-powered tool that always shows a scientist to be a white male, a poor person to be black, and an Indian person to be always an old man with a beard. Amazon’s AI-generated hiring tool systematically rooted out female applicants and so had to be rooted out itself. In the visible future, AI will not replace the imagination of the humanities – neither its good, nor its bad, and nothing in between. The question of the subjective is fundamental to the humanities, and if there is subjectivity in AI, it is created by humans, through a humanistic imagination. Nor will ideological battles and alliances vanish as long as humanity lives, it’ll be the basis of the social and the political. Ideology must be understood through humanities and the softer social sciences.

Human judgement, even when it appears to be ethical or political, often has at its core the demands of the aesthetic, which is the unique purview of the humanistic. Raghu Rai’s chillingly iconic photograph, “ Burial of an Unknown Child ”, showing the childish face sunk deep within the debris of the Bhopal gas tragedy, became the sharp symbol of the world’s greatest industrial disaster and provoked a kind of shock that hard data and scientific information about the catastrophe could not do. Closer to us is a more ludicrous spectacle. That of a certain recently concluded celebrity wedding which provoked as much ridicule from the conscientious on account of its vulgar aesthetics as from the hard numbers of the astronomic expense in a poor country. The judgement made in the domain of the aesthetic is no less potent than that made in the domain of economics.

This is going to be your domain. Own it – and the tremendous power and responsibility that come with it.

A novelist and a critic, Saikat Majumdar is Professor of English and Creative Writing at Ashoka University.

editorials.title: Millets, morels and soft power: Absurd Brics menu outrage missed India’s culinary and diplomatic triumph
editorials.passage:
I wasn’t planning to write on the Brics menu controversy, but then the debate moved to such an odd corner that one felt compelled to respond. It seems there has been quite a storm in the dinner plate over the delectable plant-based menu served at the gala at Bharat Mandapam.

Planned around India’s regional cuisine with millets the star of the show, there was mushroom galouti from Awadh, khandvi from Gujarat, morels from Kashmir, poriyal, tomato-lentil soup (Thakkali Belle Saaru) from the South, paneer from the North, Old Delhi fruit cream, phirni, that tells a tale of culinary migration from Persia — the thoughtfully designed menu took guests around the world on a culinary journey across the length and breadth of India.

Such a creative effort of marrying regional ingredients with culinary heritage deserves praise, not charges of casteism. A flippant comment or a joke or two over the lack of animal protein in the menu is understandable, but it is absolute bananas to call the showcasing of the richest vegetarian cuisine in the world that speaks of India’s incredible diversity “Brahminical Hindu-coded food preference” or “dietary despotism.”

The Congress expectedly weighed in, with Rahul Gandhi, unironically, proclaiming that “80 per cent of Indians are non-vegetarians”. It may not have struck the Gandhi scion how self-defeating his argument is. Let’s focus on the Leader of the Opposition’s statement excluding everything else.

We’ve been told Congress stands for the Nehruvian interpretation of secularism where “majoritarianism” is the biggest threat to democracy. It’s considered a ‘reactionary’, ‘disruptive’ force that militates against India’s social cohesion. Didn’t Jawaharlal Nehru write, in one of his countless letters to chief ministers, “that a minority community is a trust for the majority and constant thought should be given to its needs and complaints. In a country like India, with its great variety, this is particularly necessary”?

To claim that the Brics menu should have served a non-vegetarian menu because it presents the culinary practice of the majority of Indians is to argue in favour of majoritarianism. If that’s the position Congress has settled on, then by definition it is ‘opportunism’ that removes the cloak of virtue-signalling from Congress’s ‘pro-minority’ positions and unmasks its minorityism for what it really is, pandering to a group based on its religion for electoral benefits — far removed from any principled objection to ‘majoritarianism’.

Once again, if the Brics menu should have included meat solely because the majority of Indians are meat-eaters (a misnomer), then Congress should have had no problems when Defence Minister Rajnath Singh performed ‘shastra puja’ during the induction of Rafale fighter jets, a ritual practised by Hindus. Why did Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge call Singh’s puja “tamasha” (theatrics)? May the real Congress please stand up?

The liberals are an even stranger lot. This group claims to view climate change as an urgent crisis requiring government intervention and blames unsustainable consumer choices, such as dietary habits or heavy reliance on fossil fuels as structural behaviours accelerating global warming.

From that standpoint alone, instead of criticizing the Modi government, they should have praised New Delhi’s move to curate a plant-based menu as responsible behaviour that should be emulated by others. What we saw, unfortunately, is an inexplicable meltdown. Some suggested vegetarian dishes are threatening the “idea and meaning of India”!!
If the issue is diversity, there are better ways of displaying diversity than putting meat on the plate. There is documented evidence of meat production causing 14 per cent to 20 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions and nearly 60 per cent of all food-system emissions. Research from Stanford University points out that “from greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation to water use and pollution, meat production plays a significant role in the planet’s changing climate.”

Countless studies on similar lines indicate that the reduction of meat consumption and its substitution with plant-based alternatives have a crucial role in mitigating emissions. A paper in ScienceDirect on ‘The influence of meat consumption on greenhouse gas emissions in Argentina’ indicates a significant association between meat consumption and elevated pollution levels.

Eating your veggies doesn’t mean compromising on nutrition or health. The British Journal of Sports Medicine in 2018 reviewed dozens of studies and concluded “that there was no meaningful difference in muscle mass or strength gains between plant and animal proteins, provided individuals consumed enough protein overall—typically around 1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight per day.”

When Germany serves up plant-based meals during the G7 in the ‘interests of sustainability’, that’s kosher, while India’s vegetarian menu is an imposition of “dietary despotism”? On the contrary, India showed a way to the world for a more sustainable, responsible future, one that is in line with her citizens’ culinary habits.
Data on Indian dietary preferences reveals that India is not a strictly vegetarian nation, but a ‘flexitarian’ one where plant-based staples heavily dominate everyday meals. While national surveys like the Pew Research Center and the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5) show that only 31 per cent to 39 per cent of Indians identify as strictly vegetarian, a staggering 81 per cent of the population restricts their meat consumption in some form.

The WWF’s 2024 Living Planet Report highlights India’s food practices as a ‘model of sustainability’ and calls it the best model to follow.

The traditional Indian diet serves as a global benchmark for environmental sustainability. By preparing daily meals around grains, pulses, lentils, and vegetables rather than resource-heavy animal proteins, this predominantly plant-based model significantly minimises ecological footprints and lowers greenhouse gas emissions.
Besides, hotels where the guests have been put up created menus based on individual preferences. That includes in-room dining where non-vegetarian choices are available. For instance, Taj Mahal, New Delhi, spent months researching the culinary preferences of delegates, according to media reports. So, it’s not as if guests were made to starve if they preferred animal proteins.

The vegetarian menu at the main gala was a sensible choice for yet another reason. Non-vegetarian dietary options at such an event where guests come from various countries, religions and cultures are a complicated affair. For practicing Muslims, for instance, consuming halal meat is a mandatory act of faith. Who’s to say there wouldn’t have been controversy over whether the cuts of meat were halal or jhatka?

If the argument is that India should have kept the dietary preferences of guests at the top of the priority list above all other considerations, as some are arguing, then should we have served beef? What happens then to the ‘majoritarian’ cause?
It speaks of the crushing banality of our public discourse that it had to die on the hill of the Brics menu. At an event where India forged a consensus among withering divisions within the group, laid a roadmap for a resilient future amid global volatility and delivered a stern message to Trumpism, the national debate centred around what was served on a porcelain plate.

This myopia ignores the sheer scale of the diplomatic victory achieved by India led by the prime minister. Modi cemented his status as one of the world’s most prominent leaders by reinforcing India’s position as the definitive voice of the Global South and a key interlocutor in a divided global order.

There is no other leader in the world right now who may pull off the impossible: sharing a warm hug with Benjamin Netanyahu and a firm handshake with Masoud Pezeshkian. By forcefully widening India’s strategic space, championing the reform of global governance and leading the developing world’s shift from “rule-takers” to “rule-shapers”, Modi demonstrated his leadership skills and masterful diplomatic navigation.

The 18th edition of the Brics summit saw the prime minister leaving his indelible stamp – from the menu served at the table to stabilising India’s relationship with China, strengthening ties with Russia while carefully preserving India’s strategic ties with the West.

History may note with utter bewilderment, though, that while the world was looking at India in admiration, some Indians were busy arguing about the catering.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: Brics’ Delhi Declaration: India’s roadmap to a new world order
editorials.passage:
Set against the backdrop of a global order in decline, with a new one yet to emerge, Prime Minister Modi succeeded against all odds in positioning Brics, under India’s chairmanship, as an inclusive, but not anti-West forum.

Brics brings together eleven major emerging markets and developing countries of the world: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates.

The 18th Brics Summit concluded on September 13, 2026 in New Delhi. On September 12, the grouping adopted the “New Delhi Declaration”, under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability", marking Brics' 20th year. The 45-page Brics declaration achieved a consensus on the opening day itself, marking the coming of age of India, a balancing power, and its diplomacy.
In pragmatic and non-confrontational language, 140 paragraphs of the document covered diverse issues, including trade, health, tourism and more.
What were the more important issues in the Declaration? To list a few:

 	PM Modi proposed establishing a “Seafarers’ Emergency Support Network” to provide timely assistance and ensure the safety of personnel working at sea.
 	To keep track of the initiatives, the Prime Minister proposed a “Brics Continuity and Implementation Mechanism”, which the leaders accepted. This would enable follow-up of all initiatives and outcomes through the Troika, comprising past, current and incoming chairs.
 	Brics nations reaffirmed their commitment to enhance transport potential, including in civil aviation, while also respecting the “sovereignty and territorial integrity” of all member states. It may be noted that India, China, Russia, and Brazil are among the top-five countries in the world with the largest railway and road networks.
 	With an eye on ensuring resilient global value chains, members agreed to look at “mutually reinforcing policy levers” to boost trade within the grouping,
 	Paragraph 22 of the Declaration says the members condemn “unilateral coercive measures,” “unilateral economic sanctions and secondary sanctions”, which are references to the Western sanctions’ regimes.
 	Brics members noted that the proliferation of trade-restrictive actions is inconsistent with WTO rules, whether in the form of “indiscriminate raising of tariffs and non-tariff measures” or protectionism under the “guise of environmental objectives”.
 	Brics condemned the Pahalgam attack. On terrorism, the language was similar to the 2025 Rio Declaration. “We express strong condemnation of any acts of terrorism as criminal and unjustifiable, regardless of their motivation, whenever, wherever and by whomsoever committed. We condemn in the strongest terms the terrorist attack in Jammu and Kashmir on 22 April 2025, during which 26 people were killed and many more injured.”
 	Brics also opposed “carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM)”, aiming at US/EU trade-climate measures.
 	In the section on the UNSC, the language is similar to the 2025 Rio de Janeiro Declaration: “China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council, reiterate their support to the aspirations of Brazil and India to play a greater role in the UN, including its Security Council”.

The question arises: what issues were left out of the Delhi Declaration?
There was no mention of Ukraine. No paragraph mentions Ukraine, Russia’s invasion, or related sanctions by name. Russia’s concerns were carefully safeguarded, more than in Rio. The 2025 Rio Declaration noted: “We recall our national positions concerning the conflict in Ukraine as expressed in the appropriate fora, including the UN Security Council and the UN General Assembly.” Nor was there any language on a common Brics currency or de-dollarisation. Instead, Brics continued to focus on a more pragmatic goal by making it easier for members to promote trade settlements and investments in their own currencies to achieve faster, cheaper and safer cross-border payments.

The Declaration acknowledged discussions on promoting the use of Brics local currencies while respecting national priorities and recognising that there is “no one-size-fits-all approach”.

Before the Summit actually took place, I had somewhat pessimistic views, but my perspective changed after witnessing on TV and reading about the dynamics of the Summit and after analysing the Declaration.

My view is that this time, under India's chairmanship, India ensured that Brics was not utilised as an 'anti-Western' grouping.

It was also important to safeguard the India-US strategic partnership. The problem was that, faced with Trump's tariffs, hostility to some sections of India's diaspora and Trump’s determination to humiliate us by cosying up to Pakistan's so-called 'Field Marshal', successfully put India in a bind.

As a result, Trump has forced India to make strategic adjustments with China on trade, on people-to-people contacts, tourism etc. China too has been forced to develop a more pragmatic approach to India.

One must also underline the importance of the bilateral meetings on the margins of the Summit not just for India but for others, like the one between Iran's President and the UAE's Crown Prince.

Brics is not a replacement for the G20 or the QUAD but this time, in New Delhi, we established its relevance and, in the process, demonstrated our ability, as a balancing power, to forge a consensus between bitter adversaries on very difficult issues.

We demonstrated that even in very difficult times, we can and will hold on and, in the meantime, in the breathing space given to us, shore up our economic and military strength.

At the same time, the world stands close to a precipice of a much larger conflict. One should have no illusion of the dangerous times in which we exist, largely due to Trump.

Writing in his cell as a political prisoner in Mussolini’s fascist Italy after World War I, philosopher Antonio Gramsci famously noted in the ‘Prison Notebooks’: “The crisis consists precisely in the fact that the old is dying and the new cannot be born; in this interregnum a great variety of morbid symptoms appear.”

In a brilliant article on April 11, 2025 titled ‘Giving Birth to the New International Order’, Jeffrey D. Sachs added:
“A century later, we are in another interregnum, and the morbid symptoms are everywhere.  The US-led order has ended, but the multi-polar world is not yet born.  The urgent priority is to give birth to a new multilateral order that can keep the peace and the path to sustainable development”.

In the Brics New Delhi Declaration of 2026, it is clear that the world is slowly but surely moving to a new world order. New strategic paradigms are emerging. It also includes India becoming a ‘balancing power’. In the present state of disorder, there are few other strategic options for India.

(The author is a former Ambassador of India to the Netherlands. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: The 2026 churn that breaks tennis wide open
editorials.passage:
For a few bewildering seconds, Alexander Zverev was the only one in Arthur Ashe Stadium who didn’t realise he had won. When realisation dawned, the giant German raised his arms in celebration and fully savoured the moment that confirmed him as US Open champion. After years of promise, but agonising failure, Zverev wasn’t just a major winner; he had done it twice over — an outcome few, if any, including himself, would have predicted when the year began.

Zverev’s success, which also included a maiden run to the Wimbledon final, supplied the defining theme of the tennis year: churn.

For nine consecutive majors, beginning with the 2024 Australian Open and extending through Melbourne in 2026, every men’s singles title had been claimed by either Jannik Sinner or Carlos Alcaraz. It felt as if the trio of Federer, Nadal and Djokovic had only loosened their grip so two extraordinary young men could divide the kingdom between themselves. Theirs appeared to be a rivalry destined to define an era.

However, the tennis gods had other plans. Alcaraz’s wrist injury kept him out of Roland-Garros and Wimbledon, while Sinner suffered a shock early defeat in Paris, rebounded magnificently to retain Wimbledon, and then missed the US Open with an injury. Through the open door, 29-year-old Zverev convincingly walked in, but though he was the obvious beneficiary, he wasn’t the only one.

American Ben Shelton’s run to the final in New York was an equally consequential moment. He had always had the tools for success — an enormous left-handed serve, elastic athleticism, exuberance and the appetite for big stages. At Flushing Meadows, he added control of points, occasions and himself to his arsenal. His epic quarter-final victory over Alcaraz provided evidence that Shelton could become a more regular presence in the later stages of Slams, and even start to lift those trophies in the coming months.

When the majors come around in 2027, there is every chance that Sinner and Alcaraz, the two most naturally dominant players in the men’s game, will start to devour the titles again. However, they will be aware that the landscape has changed around them, with the likes of Zverev now entering arenas armed with the muscle memory of how to win majors and Shelton having tasted the blood of final-night energy. In essence, the psychological distance between the two standard-bearers and their pursuers has narrowed.

The women’s game experienced an even more dramatic redistribution of power. Elena Rybakina began and ended the major season as champion, defeating Aryna Sabalenka in the finals of both the Australian Open and US Open. Between those triumphs came two breakthrough winners: 19-year-old Mirra Andreeva at Roland-Garros and 21-year-old Linda Noskova at Wimbledon.

Rybakina, now a three-time major winner, stands above this shifting field, playing a brand of tennis that carries an almost eerie stillness. However, while there is a bit of daylight now between her and the rest, it certainly isn’t emptiness.

Sabalenka reached both hard-court major finals and, despite ending the year without a Slam, produced enough flashes of her most intimidating tennis to suggest that her rivalry with Rybakina could become the most compelling duel in the women’s game. Their contrast is irresistible: Sabalenka is all visible emotion and ferocious sound, while Rybakina is unflappable, yet destructive.

Behind them, the possibilities multiply. Andreeva is no longer merely a prodigy after becoming the youngest women’s champion in Paris since Monica Seles in 1992. Noskova’s Wimbledon victory transformed another promising young player into a major champion. Coco Gauff already understands how to win at that level, Naomi Osaka’s re-emergence adds both pedigree and global recognition, while Jessica Pegula and Zheng Qinwen possess the consistency and weaponry to make deep runs.

Quite visibly, 2026 has been invigorating for the sport. It started with two young men threatening to monopolise its grandest prizes and a women’s hierarchy still revolving around a familiar group. The majors wrap up with Zverev reborn, Shelton emboldened, Andreeva and Noskova crowned, Rybakina elevated and Sabalenka wounded, but unmistakably dangerous.

For tennis, this churn will supply the oxygen any modern-day sporting machine needs — an expansion of star power. Sinner and Alcaraz remain essential, but are no longer the overwhelming draw for audiences. Among the women, Rybakina may have established herself as the player to beat, but an array of champions and contenders is lined up right behind her.

So, when the Australian Open kicks off in 2027, while the leading names will return carrying reputations, their challengers will arrive carrying glittering CVs of their own. After a year in which tennis repeatedly confounded its own expectations, nobody can be entirely certain where the next celebration — or the next moment of disbelief — will come from.

(Gaurav Kalra is an award-winning sports media executive, broadcaster and content strategist with over three decades of experience telling stories from the heart of Indian and global sport.
